Tsuzumi（鼓（日本））是日本膜鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 編: The tsuzumi, listed as drum (Japan), is a Japanese membranophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 211.24. Its wooden body is hourglass-shaped, with skin at both ends joined by cords; the player squeezes or slackens the cords to change the tension of the heads and so alter the pitch while playing. It was first used by the shirabyōshi and later became the main instrument of the hayashi ensemble in Noh and kabuki; it is also used in Japanese folk song, often together with the ōtsuzumi.

小鼓（tsuzumi）主要出現在能劇與歌舞伎的伴奏樂隊中，也用於日本民間音樂。在: The small drum (tsuzumi) appears mainly in the ensemble that accompanies Noh and kabuki, and is also used in Japanese folk music. In the theatre it is often played with the ōtsuzumi and with drums such as the shimedaiko; the player strikes the head by hand and changes the pitch by squeezing or slackening the cords, which makes a short, variable rhythmic language. The sound is adjusted to the setting and the humidity, and suits the interplay of drum strokes in traditional theatre and folk song.
演奏 tsuzumi 時，先依環境溫濕度調整鼓皮：以唾液濕潤的和紙進行現場微調，: To play the tsuzumi, first adjust the heads to the temperature and the humidity: make fine adjustments on the spot with washi paper moistened with saliva, and breathe on both heads before playing so that they keep the right amount of moisture. There are two basic strokes: with the cords slack, strike the middle of the head for the softer pon and pu; with the cords squeezed, strike the head close to the body for the higher ta and chi. A beginner's task is to control the striking point, the cord tension and the moisture at the same time, and to avoid letting the skin become so wet that it slackens into ripples.

鼓的音色質感因鼓皮材質而異，通常具有溫暖而富有穿透力的特徵。鼓的音域相對較低沈，: A drum's timbre depends on the material of the head, and is usually warm and carrying. Its range is fairly low, and it can produce a deep, resonant low sound. The resonance is distinctive: the space inside the body amplifies and extends the vibration of the head, which gives a long decay. Compared with the softness of a string instrument the drum is more direct and forceful; compared with a wind instrument its timbre is steadier and heavier. The Japanese tsuzumi in particular is known for a clear, characterful stroke, hard and soft at once, which can shape fine musical expression and gives traditional Japanese music a distinctive sound.
鼓（tsuzumi）的前身腰鼓於七世紀由中國南部傳入日本，作為伎樂合奏的一部分。: The tsuzumi's predecessor, the waist drum, came to Japan from southern China in the seventh century as part of the gagaku ensemble. There were four kinds of waist drum then, and only the ichi-no-tsuzumi and the san-no-tsuzumi survive. Their heads were fixed with hemp rope, but unlike later instruments they were hung at the neck and played with a stick in the right hand and the palm of the left. In the twelfth century the smallest, the ichi-no-tsuzumi, changed to striking with the right hand and tuning with the left, and was renamed the kotsuzumi. The drum was later used by the shirabyōshi, became the main instrument accompanying Noh, and entered kabuki.

鼓（日本）為膜鳴樂器，琴身由一整塊櫻木雕成沙漏形，表面施漆與金箔蒔繪。兩面發聲體: The tsuzumi is a membranophone; the body is carved from a single block of cherry wood into an hourglass shape and finished with lacquer and gold-leaf maki-e. The two heads are of deer skin sewn onto iron rings, with a thickened reinforcing layer at the back, finished with lacquer and gold leaf, and the seam covered with lacquer as well. The tensioning system uses hemp rope, dyed with cinnabar in earlier times and now with other dyes because of its toxicity. A small leather patch is glued inside the drum to adjust the timbre. The ōtsuzumi played in the same ensemble uses a thick horsehide head with no decoration. The source does not give the materials of the remaining parts.
